title: Superlinear local certificates for hereditary graph classes
formal:
Does there exist an isomorphism-invariant hereditary class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, with connected members of arbitrarily large order, and a fixed real exponent \(c>1\), such that every correct one-round proof-labeling scheme for membership in \(\mathcal C\) has worst-case certificate size \(\Omega(n^c)\) bits per vertex on connected \(n\)-vertex inputs?

More explicitly, for the optimal accepting-certificate size \(s_A(n)\) of a fixed correct local verifier \(A\), as defined below, require
\[\exists\mathcal C\;\exists c>1\;\forall A\text{ correct for }\mathcal C\;\exists a_A>0\;\exists N_A\;\forall n\ge N_A:\ s_A(n)\ge a_A n^c.\]
The exponent and graph class are common to all verifiers. This asks for a polynomial gap above linear certificate size, not merely for a bound that grows faster than \(n\).
why: The question asks whether vertex-deletion stability imposes a fundamental information limit on distributed proofs. A polynomially superlinear example or a general obstruction would clarify how far local verification of structural graph properties can depart from the linear examples now known.
status_note: Explicitly source-open in MFCS 2024 and still explicitly asked in the full arXiv v5 revision of 24 February 2026. On 16 September 2026 the review checked both versions’ local-verifier definitions, Theorem 3.1 and the exact final superlinear question, with the current arXiv revision history confirmed. Bounded subsequent-result searches found no matching hereditary-class resolution. This is current source evidence through the checked revision, not an exhaustive certification of all later literature.

progress.text: The MFCS paper proves linear lower bounds for hereditary and monotone geometric classes and asks whether \(\Omega(n^c)\) is possible for any fixed \(c>1\).
The revised full paper retains the question and the same local-certification definitions. It does not claim a hereditary-class lower bound with exponent greater than one.

sentences: A prover gives each vertex a binary certificate, and each vertex checks only its immediate certified neighborhood.
The question asks for a hereditary graph class requiring a fixed polynomial factor more than linear certificate length at some vertex.
The lower bound must hold against every correct proof-labeling verifier and every sufficiently large graph size.
Known geometric examples require linear certificates, while a quadratic upper bound applies to all graph classes in the source model.
The February 2026 revision still asks whether any hereditary class crosses this polynomially superlinear threshold.

definitions:
A graph class is a set of finite simple undirected graphs invariant under relabelling of vertices. It is hereditary if \(G\in\mathcal C\) implies \(G[U]\in\mathcal C\) for every subset \(U\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[U]\) retains exactly the edges of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). The class is fixed independently of input size. Membership is certified only on nonempty connected input graphs, as in the source. Closure under induced subgraphs is a property of the full class, including disconnected graphs; it does not require certifying disconnected networks. Requiring arbitrarily large connected members excludes vacuous lower bounds. Such a hereditary class has connected members of every positive order, by taking connected induced subgraphs of larger connected members.

On an \(n\)-vertex input graph, each vertex has a distinct positive integer identifier from \(\{1,\ldots,n^2\}\), in binary. These are arbitrary identifiers, not part of the graph property. This fixes the source's polynomial-size identifier convention. Every completeness and soundness condition holds for every permitted identifier assignment. The prover knows the entire labelled graph and assigns a finite binary string \(\sigma(v)\in\{0,1\}^{*}\) to every vertex. Certificates may depend on the graph and its identifiers. Their cost is the maximum length at a vertex, \(\max_v|\sigma(v)|\), not the sum of all certificate lengths.

The same deterministic local verifier \(A\) is used at every vertex, on every input size and every certificate assignment. At a vertex \(v\), it sees its own identifier and certificate, and the identifiers and certificates of its immediate neighbors, with the center distinguished. It has no information about edges among neighbors, about more distant vertices, or about a geometric representation of the graph. It outputs either accept or reject. This is the one-round proof-labeling model: certificates are assigned once and examined locally, without further interaction with the prover. The graph order is not supplied as extra global information. There is no randomization or acceptance error.

As in the source's definition, a verifier and prover are mathematical functions with no computational resource bound. The quantity measures the amount of local information, not the running time of deciding a local predicate; no separate computability or recognition-time requirement is imposed on the graph class or those functions. This convention is what makes the source's universal quadratic upper bound applicable to arbitrary graph classes. A scheme must still satisfy both exact logical requirements:
\[G\in\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\sigma\;\forall v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept},\]
\[G\notin\mathcal C\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\sigma\;\exists v\in V(G):\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{reject}.\]
These quantify over every connected input and every valid identifier assignment. In the second condition the adversarial strings may be of any finite length; soundness is not restricted to certificates obeying an advertised short length. The prover is untrusted, and acceptance means that every vertex accepts.

For a fixed correct verifier \(A\) and a connected yes-instance \((G,\mathrm{id})\), let
\[\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id})=\min_{\sigma:\ \forall v\ A(v,\sigma)=\mathrm{accept}}\ \max_{v\in V(G)}|\sigma(v)|.\]
Completeness makes this a finite nonnegative integer. Define
\[s_A(n)=\max_{\substack{|V(G)|=n,\ G\in\mathcal C,\ G\text{ connected}\\ \mathrm{id}:V(G)\hookrightarrow\{1,\ldots,n^2\}}}\ell_A(G,\mathrm{id}).\]
Only finitely many labelled graphs and identifier assignments occur at a fixed \(n\), so the maximum is well-defined; if the set is empty it is defined as zero. The target's \(\Omega(n^c)\) means the displayed eventual bound for every sufficiently large integer \(n\). The verifier is fixed before taking the asymptotic limit; a different verifier for each size is not allowed. Since the prover may choose the shortest accepting certificates, this rules out cheap schemes rather than merely identifying inefficient choices of proof.

The source also asks whether the witnessing class can be monotone, meaning closed under all subgraphs obtained by deleting edges as well as vertices. Monotone classes are hereditary, so such an example would satisfy this card's main target, but edge-deletion closure is not required. The source's hereditary question is the main proposition; its stronger parenthetical variant remains context. The stronger locally-checkable-proof model additionally lets a vertex inspect the entire induced graph on its closed neighborhood. The known lower bounds in the paper hold even in that model, but the target here uses its stated proof-labeling model.

To refute the proposition, one must rule out a common positive polynomial gap for every hereditary class in the stated domain. Formally, for each such \(\mathcal C\) and each \(c>1\), there must be a correct verifier \(A\) for which \(s_A(n)\) is not \(\Omega(n^c)\): for every \(a>0\) and \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has \(s_A(n)<a n^c\). A universal near-linear upper bound would suffice, but the logical negation does not require that particular stronger result.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence statement. A positive answer must specify a hereditary class and one exponent \(c>1\), verify the closure and unbounded connected-member conditions, and prove the per-vertex lower bound against every correct verifier in the stated model, even when the prover chooses its best certificates. A negative answer must prove the logical negation for every admissible hereditary class and exponent. A linear lower bound, a bound such as \(n\log n\), a total-certificate lower bound spread over many vertices, or a lower bound for one selected verifier is insufficient. Computational hardness of centralized recognition alone is not a local certificate-size lower bound in this unrestricted-computation model. The target is an exact asymptotic proposition; numerical tolerance does not apply.

source_formulation.text: After proving the first linear local-certificate lower bounds for nontrivial hereditary and monotone graph classes, the authors ask whether some hereditary class has a lower bound with a fixed exponent strictly greater than one, and ask additionally whether it can be monotone.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the final question in MFCS 2024 §8, retained in the February 2026 full revision; the main hereditary variant is preserved

context_blocks.text: A short global proof can be difficult to verify when its readers only see neighboring pieces. Local certification asks how much evidence must be copied or distributed to individual vertices so that all honest instances are accepted and every false instance is rejected somewhere.

Hereditary properties survive deleting vertices. Many geometric intersection classes have this stability: deleting objects leaves a representation of the induced subgraph. The closure condition distinguishes this question from large lower bounds for properties that depend on a particular global size or symmetry.

The source proves linear lower bounds for several geometric classes, including penny graphs, graphs that are subgraphs of the square grid, and 1-planar graphs. These supply substantial examples at the linear threshold but do not establish a fixed exponent \(c>1\).

Theorem 3.1 bounds the local complexity of a connected graph class by \(\log_2|\mathcal C_n|+O(\log n)\), where \(\mathcal C_n\) is its set of isomorphism types with \(n\) vertices. Thus the number of possible graphs in a class gives a general information bound, and every class has an \(O(n^2)\) upper bound. The question concerns where hereditary classes can lie inside this range.

The known examples illustrate how sensitive local evidence can be to the graph property: planar graphs have logarithmic-size certificates, whereas the source proves a linear bound for 1-planar graphs. A 1-planar graph admits a drawing with at most one crossing on each edge. This comparison concerns certificate size even though local computation is unrestricted.

The full February 2026 revision retains the superlinear question. It also keeps the stronger neighborhood-inspection model separate from ordinary proof labeling. This review fixes the latter and records the stronger known lower-bound scope without changing the target.
